articles.title: Downtown on shaky ground
articles.description: Srinagar, Nov 15: Dense construction, narrow roads and closely packed buildings make downtown Srinagar the city's most vulnerable area to earthquake damage, with 23 of its 69 municipal wards falling in the high and very high vulnerability categories, a scientific study has found. Nearly 17 sq km, or about 7 percent of the city, falls in these categories. Nine wards, covering 1.28 percent of the city, were classified as very highly vulnerable and 14 wards, accounting for 5.7 percent, as highly vulnerable. Another 19 wards had moderate vulnerability, 17 low and 10 very low. High building density, narrow streets, a shortage of open spaces and the risk of buildings colliding during earthquake shaking were identified as major factors behind the vulnerability. Uptown areas were relatively less vulnerable because of wider roads and lower building density. About 65 percent of Srinagar's buildings face a high risk of structural pounding with neighbouring structures on at least one side. This occurs when closely spaced buildings strike each other during an earthquake. Nearly 98 percent of the city's buildings are masonry structures, including 86.4 percent residential and 7.1 percent commercial buildings. Educational, religious, health, defence and other structures account for the remaining 6.5 percent. Aali Kadal has the highest proportion of masonry buildings at 99.8 percent. Two-storey buildings account for 50 percent of the total and those with three or more stories 42 percent. Only 8 percent are single-storey, while 307 buildings, or 0.12 percent, have more than three floors. Downtown also has some of the city's highest building densities. Against a citywide average of 10 buildings per hectare, 17 downtown wards have more than 15. Jamia Masjid leads with 46 buildings per hectare, followed by Tarabal at 39 and Aali Kadal at 30. Bud Dal has the lowest density at one building per hectare. Narrow roads could further impede evacuation and rescue operations. Six wards — Syed Ali Akbar, Bana Mohalla, Bud Dal, Zindshah Sahib, Ganpatyar, and Safa Kadal have average road widths of less than 7 feet. The researchers linked the city's vulnerability partly to unplanned urban growth and gaps in implementing successive master plans. Srinagar's population rose from about 2.50 lakh in 1961 to 15 lakh in 2011, increasing pressure on its urban infrastructure. They recommended restricting construction in densely populated, highly vulnerable areas, protecting open spaces for emergency evacuation and retrofitting vulnerable buildings. "Since green and open spaces are used as evacuation places, it is strongly advised that new construction in these areas, as well as the development of these spaces, must be avoided," the study states. The researchers also called for emergency action plans, fire services, shelters and specialised medical facilities in vulnerable areas, along with stricter enforcement of building codes, earthquake-resistant construction and public awareness programs. The assessment covers the physical vulnerability of buildings and infrastructure but does not examine residents' socioeconomic vulnerability. The researchers recommended including these factors in future assessments. The study was conducted by Midhat Fayaz, Prof Shakil Ahmad Romshoo, Irfan Rashid, and Rakesh Chandra. Using Cartosat-2 satellite imagery, geographic information system (GIS) mapping and field surveys, they assessed six parameters across Srinagar's 69 wards and collected 8000 ground-validation points. Titled 'Earthquake vulnerability assessment of the built environment in the city of Srinagar, Kashmir Himalaya, using a geographic information system,' the study was published with funding from the Union Ministry of Earth Sciences.

articles.title: From Relief to Resilience: How Bharat transformed its disaster management
articles.description: India’s disaster management framework has undergone a significant transformation since 2014, with a growing emphasis on preparedness, prevention, risk reduction and resilience rather than relying primarily on relief and rehabilitation after disasters. Over the past decade, policy reforms, technological advancements, disaster-resilient infrastructure, community participation and increased financial allocations have contributed to strengthening the country’s ability to respond to natural calamities. The changing approach was highlighted on October 28, 2026, when Cyclone Arnab struck the Andhra Pradesh-Yanam coast. Timely weather forecasting, advance evacuation measures, coordinated government action and the rapid deployment of National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams helped minimise casualties and damage. The response reflected the importance of early-warning mechanisms, institutional coordination and preparedness in managing severe weather events. A major component of this transformation has been the development of a comprehensive institutional framework. The National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP), introduced in 2016 and aligned with the United Nations Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, established a structured approach to understanding disaster risks, strengthening governance, investing in risk reduction and improving preparedness. The Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda for Disaster Risk Reduction, presented in November 2016, further emphasised integrating disaster management into development planning and strengthening institutional capabilities. Community participation has also emerged as an important part of India’s disaster preparedness strategy. Through the Aapda Mitra scheme, the initial pilot programme covering 5,186 volunteers across 30 districts expanded towards a target of one lakh trained, certified and insured community volunteers across 350 multi-hazard-prone districts. The Yuva Aapda Mitra initiative further involved the National Cadet Corps (NCC), National Service Scheme (NSS) and Bharat Scouts and Guides in disaster preparedness and response activities. Alongside institutional and community-level reforms, India strengthened disaster-resilient infrastructure across coastal, riverine and Himalayan regions. Multi-purpose cyclone shelters, evacuation roads, bridges, underground electricity cables, saline embankments, river protection measures, slope stabilisation structures and rockfall barriers were developed to reduce the vulnerability of communities and essential infrastructure in disaster-prone areas. Technological advancements also expanded the country’s early-warning capabilities. Doppler weather radars, tsunami monitoring systems, storm-surge modelling, satellite-based drought assessment, heatwave alerts and the Damini lightning-warning application strengthened the mechanisms for identifying and communicating potential threats. Mission Mausam, approved in September 2024 with an allocation of Rs.2,000 crore, further aims to modernise weather and climate forecasting through artificial intelligence, high-performance computing and expanded radar networks. Financial assistance and emergency response mechanisms also received greater attention. During the 2021-2026 award period, Rs.1,60,153 crore was allocated to State Disaster Risk Management Funds, while Rs.54,770 crore was allocated to the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) and Rs.13,693 crore to the National Disaster Mitigation Fund (NDMF). Meanwhile, the average deployment time of Inter-Ministerial Central Teams (IMCTs) declined from 96 days to eight days by 2025, accelerating central assessment following disasters. From the introduction of institutional reforms and community-based response programmes to the expansion of early-warning technology, resilient infrastructure and financial support, these developments represent important milestones in India’s disaster management journey. The detailed From Relief to Resilience: How India Strengthened Disaster Preparedness Since 2014, is given below. India’s Progress in Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience Building India’s disaster governance system has undergone significant improvements since 2014, with a shift in focus from providing relief after disasters to strengthening preparedness, early-warning systems, risk reduction and faster emergency response. The approach has increasingly focused on minimising the loss of human lives and property through improved planning, coordination and institutional mechanisms. Before 2014, India’s disaster management system remained fragmented and largely reactive. Despite the enactment of the Disaster Management Act, 2005, disaster management authorities lacked proper coordination, adequate staffing and a unified operational plan. These shortcomings resulted in delayed responses and uncoordinated relief operations during major disasters. A significant change came in May 2016, when India introduced its first comprehensive National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP). The plan was subsequently updated in November 2019 to incorporate climate change considerations, local disaster risks and improved disaster management strategies. The NDMP aligned India’s disaster management strategy with the four priorities of the United Nations Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030. These priorities included understanding disaster risks, improving disaster management systems, investing in disaster risk reduction and strengthening preparedness for effective response. The plan also adopted the principle of Build Back Better during recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction. The implementation of this international commitment was further driven by the Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda for Disaster Risk Reduction, articulated at the Asian Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction held in New Delhi in November 2016. The agenda called for the integration of disaster risk management into the work of all development sectors. It also emphasised protecting poor households and small and medium-sized businesses, increasing women’s leadership in disaster management, and investing in multi-hazard mapping, technology and stronger institutional mechanisms. Community-Level Preparedness, Training and Public Participation The Central Government, through the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), launched the Aapda Mitra scheme to train local residents to act as first responders during disasters. Initially implemented as a pilot programme between 2016 and 2018, the scheme covered 5,186 volunteers across 30 flood-prone districts in 25 states. The scheme was subsequently expanded nationwide, with a target of training, certifying and equipping 1,00,000 community volunteers across 350 multi-hazard-prone districts in all states and Union Territories. Under the programme, volunteers receive a five-day training course conducted by master trainers from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and National Disaster Response Force (NDRF). The training covers first aid, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), basic search and rescue, navigation through collapsed structures, flood rescue operations and the evacuation of vulnerable people. Trained volunteers are provided with an Emergency Responder Kit containing protective gear, safety helmets, life jackets, LED torches, first-aid equipment, multi-tool knives and emergency whistles. Each enrolled volunteer is also provided with three years of life and disability insurance coverage. Aapda Mitra volunteers have assisted local authorities during several disasters, including Cyclone Fani in Odisha, the Kerala floods and the Wayanad landslide.
